candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: Moral truth requires a mind-grounded, nonarbitrary source, while atheism cannot justify universally binding moral values from consequences alone.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening argument is delivered by Matt after Scott explicitly asks him to present his case from the ground up.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies Matt's foundational route from truth and moral value to a transcendent source and directly challenges the secular alternative in the motion.
candidates.contextSummary: Matt develops an initial account of truth as mind-dependent, asks how moral statements obtain truth value, and argues that secular consequential assignments become arbitrary and cannot impose universal obligations.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Secular moral inquiry can begin with the substantive aim of improving well-being, while definitions themselves need not function as truth claims.
candidates.attributionBasis: Scott takes the floor after Matt yields and explicitly contrasts top-down and bottom-up approaches while explaining his own practical moral concern.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move presents a secular alternative to Matt's proposed foundation and answers the charge that defining morality through welfare is an arbitrary truth claim.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt's claim that secular welfare-based morality lacks truth value and becomes arbitrary.

candidates.contextSummary: Scott distinguishes conceptual analysis from a bottom-up inquiry focused on happiness, flourishing, and avoidable suffering, then argues that a moral definition is not itself the proposition requiring truth evaluation.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: Morality is grounded in God's immutable character rather than arbitrary divine commands, and goodness is known through God's self-revelation.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matt expressly rejects the divine-command formulation attributed to him and states the character-based Christian account during the ensuing exchange.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the principal pro-side specification of how God grounds morality and is essential to distinguishing Matt's view from arbitrary command theory.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Scott's formulation that moral and immoral acts are respectively commanded or forbidden by God.

candidates.contextSummary: Matt rejects arbitrary command theory, identifies God's nature and essence as the moral standard, and says humans discover goodness because the eternal divine character is revealed to them.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Defining goodness by God's actual attributes leaves no independent basis for judging those attributes good and therefore makes morality arbitrary or accidental.
candidates.attributionBasis: Scott leads the questioning throughout this passage, identifies the absence of an external standard, and develops the dishonest-God counterfactual in his own turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move presses the central arbitrariness objection against a divine-nature theory even after arbitrary divine-command theory has been disclaimed.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt's claim that God's immutable character is the standard of goodness disclosed through revelation.

candidates.contextSummary: Scott argues that calling honesty good merely reports that God happens to be honest, then asks whether God controls his character and whether a divine nature of dishonesty is genuinely impossible.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Appealing only to God's fixed identity does not explain why a contrary divine nature is impossible, so the divine standard remains modally unexplained.
candidates.attributionBasis: Scott repeatedly advances and refines the possible-world and hypothetical-world challenge, with Matt's short answers serving as the objects of that sustained examination.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This develops the arbitrariness objection into a modal challenge about whether God's moral character has any reason or necessity beyond bare identity.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt's answer that God cannot lie because dishonesty conflicts with God's revealed, unchanging nature.

candidates.contextSummary: Scott distinguishes God's inability to change from the possibility of an eternally different nature, challenges identity-based answers as circular, and constructs a world where opposite divine traits set opposite moral standards.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: A counterfactual that reverses God's essential character cannot adjudicate divine morality because it abandons the very theological principles under examination.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matt directly answers the proposed alternate divine nature, explains why he will not grant it, and concludes by restating his revealed-character account.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Matt's principal response to the modal arbitrariness challenge and defends the necessity of the divine nature underlying his moral foundation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Scott's hypothetical world in which God's immutable traits are dishonest and hateful rather than honest and loving.

candidates.contextSummary: Matt declines to reason from a scenario that contradicts God's holiness, distinguishes a truth-related thought experiment from redefining God, and grounds objective morals in God's actual righteous character and revelation.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: If God is the sole standard used to evaluate God, believers cannot noncircularly determine whether that standard is good rather than profoundly harmful.
candidates.attributionBasis: Scott clarifies the counterfactual, tests dishonesty for logical impossibility, and then explicitly states the circular-standard objection as the conclusion of his questioning.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument directly disputes whether God can provide a rationally evaluable necessary foundation for morality rather than merely a self-certifying standard.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt's insistence that God's actual immutable holiness and internal logical consistency exclude a dishonest divine nature.

candidates.contextSummary: Scott separates an eternally different nature from a change in nature, argues that lying is not logically impossible in itself, and concludes that Matt lacks a standard independent of God for recognizing divine goodness.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: A divine-nature account supplies no rational reason to obey God because its justification that God is good collapses back into conformity with God's nature.
candidates.attributionBasis: Scott supplies the extended practical example and carries it through the successive questions about wrongness, divine nature, goodness, and reasons for compliance.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This converts the circularity critique into a challenge about normative authority, addressing whether a divine foundation can generate reasons and obligations for agents.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt's position that humans lack the standing or sufficient knowledge to judge God's morality.

candidates.contextSummary: Using a disputed sexual prohibition, Scott traces the proposed justification from wrongness to God's nature and then to God's goodness, arguing that the circular definitions leave the commanded person without a rational reason to comply.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: God's omniscience distinguishes divine moral revelation from human judgment because God knows every actual and potential consequence relevant to action.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matt responds immediately to Scott's practical objection and explicitly invokes divine omniscience to distinguish God from an ordinary human adviser.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response offers an epistemic basis for divine moral authority and introduces complete knowledge of consequences as an answer to the comparison with human standards.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Scott's claim that God's nature is unevaluable and therefore provides no rational basis for obedience.

candidates.contextSummary: Matt says Scott's reasoning leads toward moral agnosticism, contrasts limited human knowledge with God's knowledge of all actual and possible facts, and argues that divine prescriptions may rest on reasons humans cannot fully understand.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: If omniscience makes God morally authoritative by supplying otherwise unavailable facts, then access to those facts could remove the need for God as the standard.
candidates.attributionBasis: Scott explicitly identifies Matt's invocation of omniscience, frames its relevance as a new question, and reaches the stated implication at the final owned-core row.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move tests whether the proposed divine foundation is genuinely constitutive of morality or merely an informational substitute for facts humans presently lack.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt's claim that God's exhaustive knowledge gives divine revelation moral authority unavailable to ordinary humans.

candidates.contextSummary: Scott asks why omniscience makes God a better moral standard than an ordinary person and whether God functions only as a source of facts which, if independently known, would make divine authority unnecessary.
